unit: per job: the valve cover (cylinder head cover) gasket set. One cover on inline engines. On V engines the range runs from one bank to both banks, as noted per class. Not included: a new valve cover, intake manifold gaskets where the manifold has to come off, spark plugs or ignition coils. On some engines with plastic covers (several BMW and Volkswagen engines) the cover is commonly replaced as a whole or the gasket is only sold with it; that costs far more and is noted in the luxury class

finding: The live range of $150-$950 looks about right. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2014 Chevrolet Cruze 1.4L about $97-$529 (0.6-3 hr); midsize 2015 Accord V6 about $153 for the rear bank only (1.1 hr) to about $404 for both banks (2.2 hr); truck 2017 F-150 3.5L EcoBoost, both covers, about $548-$860 (4.2-4.4 hr); luxury 2018 Lincoln Navigator 3.5L EcoBoost, both covers, about $548-$828 (4.2 hr). The $97 figure pairs GM's 0.6-hour warranty time with a $25 aftermarket gasket and no diagnosis time, so it is a floor that few real quotes will reach; with the 1.3 hours one mechanic's guide calls typical for an inline four the Cruze comes to about $180-$260, in line with the $150 floor. At the top, the two twin-turbo V6 examples reach about $830-$860 with gaskets only, and about $1,040 if the complete covers are replaced as Ford's bulletin does ($368 for the pair at list plus 4.2 hours at $160); the earlier luxury example, a 2015 BMW 328i, came to about $963 with a whole new plastic cover ($482.85 kit plus 3 hours at $160). One mechanic's guide puts a 2015 Ford Explorer 3.5L at $980-$1,100 and YourMechanic lists a 2015 Volvo S80 at $1,575, so some vehicles will exceed the live top. The range is wide because the job really does vary: the gasket is cheap ($20-$156 here) and almost all of the cost is labor, which runs from well under an hour on an easy inline four to more than four hours where an intake manifold and turbo plumbing must come off. How solid the labor times are: four of the seven distinct figures are manufacturer warranty times for the example vehicle itself. Economy: the example was changed from a 2015 Toyota Corolla to a 2014 Chevrolet Cruze 1.4L because GM prints a time; GM allows 0.6 hours to replace the camshaft cover on the Cruze in two special-coverage bulletins (plus up to 0.5 or 1.0 hour of diagnosis). The high end (3 hours) is a general statement about inline fours, not a Cruze time. Midsize: the low end is Honda's warranty flat-rate time of 1.1 hours for the rear bank of the Accord V6, and that procedure also replaces intake manifold gaskets that we did not price; the high end (2.2 hours) is a named mechanic's figure for an Acura with a similar 3.5L V6. Truck: the example was changed from a 2016 Silverado 5.3L V8 to a 2017 F-150 3.5L EcoBoost because Ford states 4.2 hours to replace both valve covers on that truck (4.4 hours on the Raptor). The earlier figure of 1.7-1.9 hours came from a cost guide's customer rows for V8 trucks and SUVs; a pushrod V8 is a much shorter job than this engine, so V8 truck owners should expect less (the earlier built total for the Silverado was about $213-$322), but no manufacturer time was found to pin that down. Luxury: the example was changed from a 2015 BMW 328i to a 2018 Lincoln Navigator because BMW bulletins refer dealers to BMW's own labor system instead of printing a time; Ford states 4.2 hours for both covers on the Navigator, the only stated time found, so both ends of the range are that one figure. The Navigator uses the same engine as the truck example, so the luxury class is not an independent check, and it should not be read as the price for a European luxury car. All the Ford and GM times are for replacing the complete cover, which is the same removal and refitting work as a gasket job. They are warranty times, the low end of what shops bill. Parts caveats: for the Ford engine only the passenger-side genuine gasket has a list price ($43.83), the driver-side gasket is listed without one, and the high figure is an aftermarket set for both covers; on the Accord the genuine gasket at list is cheaper than the aftermarket set, so the low end is a genuine part. A Hyundai campaign bulletin (2007-2009 Santa Fe 3.3L, front bank gasket plus alternator test and oil protector) allows 1.3 hours, which supports the low end for one bank of a V6; the Hyundai Veracruz recall 14V-415 documents on file do not print a time. Our economy and midsize totals sit a little below RepairPal ($375-$514); its labor figure of $288-$423 implies about two to three hours at typical rates, more than the warranty and easy-engine times at our low ends. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): the luxury class was put back to the 2015 BMW 328i (general 1-3 hr, about $158-$546 built) because a Lincoln Navigator sharing the truck engine and one Ford time used for both ends added nothing new; the Ford 4.2 hr Navigator time is covered by the truck class. Truck parts low is one genuine gasket (the other side has no listed price) while the hours cover both covers, so the truck low is slightly understated. Confidence stays low: half of the hour figures are general.
extras: A quote often adds spark plug tube seals and cover bolt grommets if the set does not include them, spark plugs or ignition coils that have been soaked in oil, intake manifold gaskets on engines where the manifold comes off to reach the rear cover, engine cleaning to confirm the leak has stopped, shop supplies and sales tax. On V engines the second bank is usually quoted at the same time. A PCV valve built into the cover, or a cracked or warped plastic cover, can turn the job into a whole-cover replacement costing several hundred dollars more. An oil leak diagnosis fee may be charged separately.
